content: Acute sinusitis is typically triggered by a preceding upper respiratory tract infection, which is most often viral in origin. The viral damage to the mucosal surfaces creates an environment conducive to bacterial colonization. The most common bacterial pathogens involved are Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Staphylococcus aureus. Other bacterial culprits may include various Streptococcus species, anaerobic bacteria, and, less frequently, gram-negative bacteria. In some cases, dental issues affecting the maxillary sinus can also lead to sinusitis. Additionally, acute sinusitis can result from fungal infections, which are more commonly observed in individuals with diabetes or other forms of immune compromise, such as those with AIDS or transplant recipients on immunosuppressive therapy. These fungal infections can be life-threatening. In type I diabetes, sinusitis caused by fungal invasion, specifically Mucormycosis, is associated with ketoacidosis. Chronic sinusitis represents a complex spectrum of diseases characterized by persistent inflammation of the sinuses. The etiology is multifactorial and may include allergies, environmental factors such as dust or pollution, bacterial infections, and fungal involvement, which can be allergic, infectious, or reactive in nature. Non-allergic conditions, such as vasomotor rhinitis, can also contribute to chronic sinus problems. The symptoms of chronic sinusitis include nasal congestion, facial pain, headache, fever, general malaise, thick green or yellow nasal discharge, a sensation of facial fullness that worsens when bending forward, and aching teeth. In rare cases, chronic sinusitis can lead to anosmia, the loss of the ability to smell or detect odors. Occasionally, chronic maxillary sinusitis may arise from the spread of bacteria from a dental infection. Efforts have been made to standardize the classification of chronic sinusitis subtypes. The American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery/Foundation, in collaboration with the Sinus and Allergy Health Partnership, has divided chronic sinusitis into two primary categories: chronic sinusitis without polyps and chronic sinusitis with polyps, the latter often referred to as chronic hyperplastic sinusitis. Recent research has sought to better understand the pathological progression of chronic sinusitis, leading to the proposal of additional subtypes. Many patients exhibit eosinophilic infiltration in the mucosal lining of the nose and paranasal sinuses, giving rise to the term eosinophilic mucin rhinosinusitis (EMRS). While some cases of EMRS may be linked to allergic responses, allergy is not always documented, resulting in further subcategorization into allergic and non-allergic EMRS. A more recent and still debated development in chronic sinusitis research is the potential role of fungi. Fungi are frequently found in the nasal cavities and sinuses of patients with sinusitis, but they are also present in healthy individuals. It remains uncertain whether fungi are a definitive factor in the development of chronic sinusitis and, if so, what distinguishes those who develop the disease from those who do not.
